result:
In the quiet hum of a morning I once spent in a small café, the scent of freshly brewed coffee mingled with the faint aroma of cinnamon from the pastries. Outside, the world was waking up—birds chirping, distant laughter, the occasional honk of a car. I sat there, notebook in hand, watching the world through the steam rising from my cup. Life, I thought, is like that coffee: warm, comforting, but always changing.

I’ve always been drawn to the idea of impermanence. The way a flower wilts, the way a friendship fades, the way even the strongest emotions dissolve into memory. There’s a beauty in it, a kind of poetry. We cling to things—people, places, moments—but they’re never ours to keep. And yet, that’s what makes them precious. The fear of losing something makes us appreciate it more.

I wonder if we’re all just passing through, like leaves on a river. Some drift quickly, some linger longer, but none stay forever. Maybe that’s why we create—art, music, stories—to capture the fleeting, to say, *This was real. This mattered.* But even those creations fade. A painting yellows, a song gets forgotten, a book gets left on a shelf.

Yet, in the fading, there’s stillness. A quiet acceptance that everything is temporary, and that’s okay. The world keeps turning, and we keep turning with it. Maybe the goal isn’t to hold on but to dance in the moment, to feel the warmth of the sun, the weight of the wind, the laughter of strangers. To live, not as if we have all the time in the world, but as if every second is a gift.

And so, I sip my coffee, watching the steam curl into the air. The world is vast, and I’m just a small part of it. But in this small part, there’s wonder.
